'''Edward Curtis Taylor, Jr.''' (August 3, 1923 – November 22, 2017) was an American chemist who designed and synthesized the [[chemotherapy]] drug [[pemetrexed]] (brand name Alimta), an inhibitor of purine biosynthesis, with grant support from the U.S. National Cancer Institute, NIH. As of 2009, [[royalties]] for this drug from Eli Lilly & Co. paid to [[Princeton University]] were sufficient to completely finance a state-of-the-art {{convert|263000|sqft|m2|adj=on}} chemistry laboratory building.<ref name="PAW2009">{{cite journal|title=It all began with butterflies|author=[[Shirley M. Tilghman]]|date=April 1, 2009|journal=[[Princeton Alumni Weekly]]|volume=109|issue=11|page=2}}</ref> Taylor studied for his PhD from 1946 to 1949 at Cornell University with Professor Cornelius Cain. Taylor trained 187 PhD students.

==Biography==
He was born in [[Springfield, Massachusetts]] on August 3, 1923. He had first enrolled at Hamilton College then transferred to Cornell<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wippman |first1=David |title=Generous Donor, Renowned Chemist Edward Taylor '46 Dies |url=https://www.hamilton.edu/news/story/generous-donor-renowned-chemist-edward-taylor-46-dies |website=Hamilton |access-date=30 July 2022}}</ref> and received both his B.A. in 1946 and then his Ph.D. in 1949, both from [[Cornell University]]. He was a Merck Postdoctoral Fellow from 1949 to 1950 at the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in [[Zürich, Switzerland]] under [[Leopold Ruzicka]]. He was a du Pont Postdoctoral Fellow at the [[University of Illinois]] from 1950 to 1951.<ref>{{cite web|title=Edward C. Taylor, Ph.D.: Curriculum Vitae|publisher=Princeton University|url=https://www.princeton.edu/~chemdept/ECT/cv.html|accessdate=2009-04-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170928155753/http://www.princeton.edu/~chemdept/ECT/cv.html|archive-date=2017-09-28|url-status=dead}}</ref> 
He was the A. Barton Hepburn Professor of Organic Chemistry, Emeritus, joined the Princeton faculty in 1954 and transferred to emeritus status in 1997.

In 2006 Taylor was named a [[Heroes of Chemistry|Hero of Chemistry]] by the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2017/11/29/princeton-chemist-edward-c-taylor-inventor-anti-cancer-drug-dies-94 |title=Princeton chemist Edward C. Taylor, inventor of anti-cancer drug, dies at 94 |access-date=2017-11-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191030073702/https://www.princeton.edu/news/2017/11/29/princeton-chemist-edward-c-taylor-inventor-anti-cancer-drug-dies-94 |archive-date=2019-10-30 |url-status=live }}</ref> 

He died on November 22, 2017.
